title: One small step at a time: Euler's method

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the hatched drift between the straight steps and the faint exact curve shrinking as you choose smaller step sizes for the capacitor's discharge.
interactive.title: The stepper
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This is a short lesson in thirteen small screens. A 100 µF capacitor charged to 12 V discharges through a 10 kΩ resistor. So τ = RC = 1 s. Its rule is dV/dt = −V ÷ 1, in volts and seconds. Voltage runs up the side, from 0 to 12 V. Time runs along the bottom, from 0 to 3 s. A faint slope field fills the plot. A faint exact curve, V = 12 e^(−t), runs through it. Euler's method walks on top. At each point it reads the arrow there. It walks straight along it for one step size h. Then it reads again. So new value = old value + h × slope at the old value. The gap between the walk and the curve is hatched. That is the drift. Screen 1 starts a dot at 12 V. The arrow there slopes −12 V a second. The dot walks 0.5 s along it, down to 6 V. Screen 2 asks where the next 0.5 s step lands. The choices are 3 V, 0 V or 4.41 V. Screen 3 draws both steps and the curve. At 1 s the walk reads 3 V and the curve 4.41 V. The drift of 1.41 V is hatched. Short tangent ticks along the first step show the curve easing off while the step keeps its starting slope. Screen 4 asks where 0.25 s steps are at 0.5 s. The choices are 6.75 V, 7.28 V or 6 V. Screen 5 offers a named choice of step size: 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 or 1 s. It opens on 0.5 s. Each step's starting arrow is drawn where it begins, so every step is seen to use the slope at its start. A table logs the value at 1 s for each step size chosen, beside the curve's 4.41 V. The rows read 4.30, 4.18, 3.80, 3.00 and 0 V. Their drifts are 0.11, 0.23, 0.62, 1.41 and 4.41 V. As the steps shrink, the value at 1 s climbs towards 4.41 V. On a phone the table's columns wrap. Screen 6 asks the drift with 0.05 s steps, given 0.23 V with 0.1 s steps. The choices are about 0.11 V, about 0.23 V or about 0.06 V. The 0.05 s row stays hidden until he checks. Screen 7 widens the plot to run from −12 to 12 V and from 0 to 6 s. A named choice offers 1, 1.5 or 2 s steps. A dashed line marks the steady state at 0 V. Each step adds h × (−V ÷ τ), so it multiplies the value by 1 − h ÷ τ. With 1 s steps the walk drops to 0 V at 1 s and stays there. With 1.5 s steps it goes 12, −6, 3, −1.5 and 0.75 V. It swings either side of 0 V and dies away. With 2 s steps it goes 12, −12, 12 and −12 V, for ever. The curve itself never crosses 0 V. Screen 8 asks the first 1.5 s step from 12 V. The choices are −6 V, 0 V or 2.68 V. Screen 9 swaps in a tank. Its level h obeys dh/dt = 0.3 − 0.2 √h, in metres and minutes. It fills from empty. Level runs up the side, from 0 to 2.5 m, and time along the bottom, from 0 to 20 min. A dashed line marks the steady level, 2.25 m. There is no faint curve, because this rule has no tidy formula. A named choice offers steps of 2, 1, 0.5 or 0.25 min. Each walk is drawn on top of the others. Readouts log the level at 4 min: 0.89, 0.79, 0.75 and 0.73 m. Each halving moves the answer less. Screen 10 asks one 1 min step from 1 m. The choices are 1.1 m, 1.3 m or 0.1 m. Screens 11 to 13 mix it all. Screen 11 steps the coil from the last lesson, di/dt = (24 − 10 i) ÷ 0.5, from 0 A, in two steps of 0.01 s. The choices are 0.864 A, 0.96 A or 0.791 A. Screen 12 shows the same coil stepped with 0.075 s steps. Its current reads 0, 3.6, 1.8 and 2.7 A. It asks why. The choices are: the step is longer than τ, so it overshoots; the current really rings; or the steady value is 3.6 A. Screen 13 shows the tank at 4 min reading 0.79 m with 1 min steps and 0.75 m with 0.5 min steps. It asks what to do next. The choices are: halve the step again and compare; take 0.79 m; or average them to 0.77 m. Each puzzle offers three answers.
interactive.ignores: The steps are drawn slowed down and much larger than a computer would take. A computer also rounds each number a little, and this lesson leaves that out. The capacitor and resistor are ideal. The tank's rule is an example rule, with its outflow growing as the square root of the level. A real tank's outflow depends on its outlet. Euler's method is the simplest stepper. Textbooks add that better ones read the slope more than once in each step.

explain.text:
Euler's method solves a rule by walking it. Stand at the start. Read the slope the rule gives there. Walk a short straight step along it. Then read the slope again where you land, and repeat.[^1] It needs no formula, only the rule. So it works on rules that have none.

Take the capacitor from before, now with 10 kΩ. So τ = RC = 1 s. Its rule is dV/dt = −V ÷ 1. At 12 V the slope is −12 V a second. Walk 0.5 s along it and you fall 6 V, to 6 V. At 6 V the slope is −6 V a second. So the next 0.5 s takes you to 3 V. Each step is new value = old value + h × slope, where h is the [[step size]]. That is [[Euler's method]].

Now compare. The exact curve reads 4.41 V at 1 s, but the walk reads 3 V. The reason is in each step. A step keeps the slope it read at its start. Along the step the voltage falls, so the true slope eases off. The straight line does not. So it falls too far, and the walk drifts below the curve. Shorter steps re-read the slope more often. So a smaller step gives a better answer and a larger one a worse answer.[^3] At 1 s, 0.1 s steps give 4.18 V and 0.05 s steps give 4.30 V. Halving the step roughly halved the drift here.

Too big a step does worse than drift. Each step adds h × (−V ÷ τ) to V. So each step multiplies the voltage by 1 − h ÷ τ. With 1.5 s steps that is −0.5. The first step reads −12 V a second and walks for 1.5 s. It falls 18 V, straight past 0 V to −6 V. Then it swings back. The real voltage never goes below 0 V, so the swing comes only from the steps. With 2 s steps it swings for ever. In a rule like these, the rate depends only on the value. Then the true curve cannot cross its steady line. So a walk that swings across it is taking steps that are too big.

The same walk works where no formula exists. Take a tank filled at a steady rate that drains through its base. Say its level h obeys dh/dt = 0.3 − 0.2 √h, in metres and minutes. Its steady level is where the two balance, at 2.25 m. You cannot rearrange this rule into a tidy formula for h against time. So step it, then halve the step and step again. From empty, the level at 4 min reads 0.89 m with 2 min steps. Then 0.79 m, 0.75 m and 0.73 m as the steps halve. Each halving moves the answer less. When it barely moves, you can trust it.

**Euler's method walks short straight steps along the rule's slope, re-reading it after each one. Smaller steps drift less from the true curve. For a decay, steps longer than the time constant overshoot.**

analogy.text: It is dead reckoning. You know where the boat is, its course and its speed. Run on that course for a set time and mark the new position. Then take the new course and speed and run again. Long runs between updates drift further from the true track.
analogy.breaks: A navigator's course is set by the helm, not by where the boat is. Euler's slope changes with the value itself. And a navigator gets fixes that reset the error. Euler's method never gets one, so its drift is only kept small by short steps.

practice.text:
- Write the rule as slope = f(value, time).
- Choose a step size h. For a decay, start well under the time constant.
- Find the slope at the start.
- New value = old value + h × slope. New time = old time + h.
- Find the slope at the new value, and repeat.
- Halve h and run it again. If the answer barely moves, trust it.

**Rules of thumb:** steps of a tenth of τ gave a value about 5% low at one τ here. For a decay, steps longer than τ overshoot the steady state. A spreadsheet does this well, with one row per step.

**Worked example:** take the coil from before, di/dt = (24 − 10 i) ÷ 0.5, starting at 0 A. Use steps of 0.01 s. The starting slope is 24 ÷ 0.5 = 48 A a second. So after 0.01 s, i = 0 + 0.01 × 48 = 0.48 A. The slope there is (24 − 4.8) ÷ 0.5 = 38.4 A a second. So after 0.02 s, i = 0.48 + 0.384 = 0.864 A. The exact formula gives 0.791 A. The walk runs high, because this curve flattens as it rises and each step keeps its steeper starting slope.

**Common mistakes**
- Reusing the starting slope for every step. Re-read it at each new value.
- Expecting the steps to land on the exact curve. They drift from it, and the drift builds up.
- Adding the slope instead of h × slope.
- Trusting a walk that swings either side of its steady line. Shrink the step.
- Trusting one run. Halve the step and compare.
